source.title: Predicting Deep Neural Network Generalization with Perturbation Response Curves
source.authors: Yair Schiff; Brian Quanz; Payel Das; Pin-Yu Chen

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendix supplied
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether perturbation-response statistics predict train–test generalization gaps using a different measure; it does not test the claim’s memorization, optimizer, batch-size or regularization comparisons directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own PR-curve accuracy under interpolation and image transformations, and CMI scores showing how well derived measures predict generalization gaps. Rows capture these measurements and the reported predictive scores. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates predictors of generalization gaps, but none measures a listed version. Its perturbations modify inputs or hidden representations, not weights scaled by their magnitudes as V7 requires. Varying batch size and using Adam are experimental settings, without reported comparisons testing V4 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that PR-derived Gi and Pal scores competitively predict generalization gaps, and that Gi-score helps assess invariance to specified transformations. Predictive performance depends on the task and score configuration; theoretical guarantees and evaluation beyond image tasks remain future work.
record.recipe_differences: Post hoc prediction and measurement of generalization using PR curves and CMI, rather than interventions on memorization, width, architecture comparisons, optimizers, batches, regularizers, sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive usefulness varies by architecture, dataset, perturbation type and layer; the authors report different useful score variants across architectures. Gi-score CMI varies with perturbation type, architecture, dataset, and training augmentation conditions. Sample size affects reported CMI variability.

fits_no_version.finding: Gi and Pal statistics derived from interpolation response curves predict generalization gaps with performance that varies across tasks, layers, and score combinations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input- and representation-perturbation response statistics provide task-dependent information about generalization gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: Gi-score has the highest CMI among the three tested predictors in 14 of 16 transformation settings; exceptions are CIFAR-10 VGG rotation and SVHN VGG color jittering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gi-score often predicts generalization gaps on transformed test sets better than augmented-training-subset accuracy or mean perturbation-response accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report that variability of Gi-score CMI becomes relatively small as more evaluation batches are sampled.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sufficient evaluation sampling stabilizes perturbation-response generalization predictors.

record.problems: The experiments focus on image datasets and prediction scores rather than direct causal interventions on generalization mechanisms. The authors state that the approach currently lacks theoretical underpinning. Table 1's numerical results are task aggregates; the invariance analysis restricts to models attaining at least 80% training accuracy. Several sensitivity results are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No required result rows omitted. Appendix combination tables 4–9 contain additional combinations of the paper’s measures; they are not separately extracted because the key comparison rows are represented by Table 1 and these combinations do not test a listed version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out performance, and chance-level random-label held-out performance.
Test-error changes with width beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under limited or broader tuning.
Held-out performance comparisons across training batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout's effect on test error across training-set sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No listed version is tested, so no verdict labels apply. Nearly perfect training accuracy alone does not test V1, and a predictive association involving input perturbations does not test V7.

versions.untested_parts: Whether architectures fitting random labels generalize on natural labels, and random-label test accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and their test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization comparisons.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer held-out performance comparisons.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout intervention and its effect on test error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
